184: What is real and what is simulated
185: Real terrain and shadows: topography of the rim of Shackleton crater (LOLA/LRO, NASA, 10 m per pixel), 3.2 km around the station. The rest of the crater seen in the distance is an approximate model, only for context.
186: Simulated ice: the permanent shadows are calculated from the real terrain; the ice inside them is simulated.
187: Light: at the pole the Sun is only ~1° above the horizon. The “fill light” lights from above only so the terrain is easier to see.
188: Real sky: 62,000 stars from NASA maps (Gaia and Hipparcos data); the Milky Way appears through its star density, with a very faint blue veil (aesthetic). With “Long-exposure sky” they look like a long-exposure photo; turn it off to see the sky as the eye would with the ground lit.
189: The Earth is made with NASA satellite images, in its real direction and phase as seen from Shackleton. “Earth view” shows it through a telephoto lens, as in real photos.
190: Rocks and regolith: photographic scans (Poly Haven, CC0).
191: Drilling: the cutaway view next to the drill bit is illustrative; the thickness of the dry layer and the ice percentage are the model's values at that point, and the cuttings fall under lunar gravity.
192: Rover: the exploded view shows the rover's own design. The map and telemetry data come from the simulation model.
193: Design assumptions: the UKU PACHA MK-I colony has 10 people (expandable in stages) who each use ~2.5 L of water a day and recycle 90% (they need ~2.5 L/day of new water). The rover moves at 3.6 km/h (NASA's VIPER moves at ~0.8 km/h), with a 300 W drill and a 1200 W charger at the station. Regenerating the chemical filter in the oven is a hypothesis.
228: Regenerate the chemical filter in the oven (hypothesis)
229: When the oven is free, or little filter is left, it heats the filter to clean and reuse it. Each cycle loses 10% (assumption).
230: How the water is obtainedIn a vacuum, ice does not melt: when heated above ~210 K it turns straight into vapour. The vapour freezes in the cold trap (the box that gets covered in frost). Then it is melted, passes through the microorganism biofilter (the dome), then through chemical filters and a membrane with UV light, and reaches the blue tank.
231: The water that comes out of lunar ice carries ammonia, sulphur, methanol and mercury. Before the chemical filters, it goes through a sealed biofilter where these microorganisms clean it.

253: What is real and what is hypothesisHeat turns the ice into vapour; microorganisms cannot do that. Their role is to clean the water. That bacteria of the genus Deinococcus reduce mercury and that lichens detect sulphur is documented. That these particular species can do it in a lunar biofilter is a hypothesis that must be tested in the lab. The values are illustrative.

271: Yes, in parts. None of them combines the same pieces as ICEWISE.
273: It extracted, captured and purified water from icy simulated lunar soil, in a vacuum and with up to 13 kg per test. Its cleaning chain combined microfiltration, reverse osmosis, activated carbon and ion exchange. It reached readiness level 4 (validated in the lab). It is the closest thing to our plant.
275: Paragon Space showed that a cold trap separates water from part of the contaminants. NASA is testing membrane bioreactors that use bacteria to remove ammonia from spacecraft water, the same idea as our biofilter.
277: Combining a rover that searches and decides where to drill, the extraction plant, a biofilter with radiation-resistant organisms and delivery to a colony at Shackleton. All within one system and simulated on the real topography.
